rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3-5, Figs 2, 9-16 report the authors' own LAI field campaigns, eddy-covariance validation, comparisons of advised vs metered irrigation volumes and farmer feedback in three service areas. Q2: Section 5.1 and Abstract - the authors state that adoption of the IRRISAT webGIS/SMS advisory produced an increase of irrigation efficiency through reduction of applied volumes compared with traditional practice; Figs 10-11 compare suggested and metered applied volumes (farmers apply ~15% more than advised); Section 5.2 Fig 13-14 shows standard FAO Kc would over-irrigate relative to satellite-based plot-specific CWR; farmers in all areas rated the plot-level, timely information positively. Q4: Figs 9, 12, 15 compare satellite LAI with Licor LAI-2000 field measurements (R2 0.85, RMSE 0.42 in 2013) and Fig 2 compares ETcrop from Eq. (3) with eddy-covariance fluxes in corn and alfalfa, i.e. the intermediate variables (LAI, ETcrop) through which the advisory affects water use. Q5: Sections 5.1-5.3 report results separately for Campania (Italy, herbaceous crops), Marchfeld (Austria, sugarbeet, semi-arid), and Bookpurnong (South Australia, citrus/vines). Q6: Fig 11 compares measured and advised volumes for the 1200-ha Boscariello district; Table 2 covers 5500 ha and 669 farmers; Section 5.2 compares scheme-level CWR with volumes distributed in the Marchfeld area; Section 5.3 reports farm-scale cumulative volumes. Q7: Section 5.1 - from their own experience, the authors state that in small farms efficiency is lower and farmers reluctant to adopt IRRISAT, attributing it to limited economic resources, dated equipment and the absence of metering-based water pricing, whereas farms above 10-12 ha adopt the advice; Section 6 states that user feedback is essential for effectiveness in water-use optimisation. Q8: Section 5.1 - comparison with actual volumes is often difficult due to scarce field data; over-irrigation partly due to lag between advice and application; Section 5.2 - detailed crop management and soil data missing so interpretation is speculative, satellite data did not cover the whole season; Section 5.3 - comparison excludes rainfall and further validation is needed.
rows.notes: Q2 is weak: the water-saving result is largely asserted ('it was proven'); the traditional-volume figures (4500-6000 m3/ha maize) come from local water managers' estimates, and the metered comparisons show farmers applying about 15% more than advised rather than a measured before/after reduction. Q3 no: water saving is not established by two independent methods (farmer feedback concerns usefulness, not savings; volume comparison is one method). Q7 is borderline: farm size/metering are stated as explanations of differential adoption rather than explicit requirements. Q9 no: no SD/CI/range for the water-saving result; Fig 16 <U+00B1>SD refers to citrus Kc and LAI RMSE is a validation error.

rows.evidence: Q1: as above - own LAI campaigns, eddy-covariance validation, volume comparisons in three regions. Q2: Section 3 and Fig 2 - the authors derive ETcrop and an 'analytical' Kc from satellite LAI/albedo and validate ETcrop against eddy-covariance in corn and alfalfa; Section 5.2 Figs 13-14 - satellite-based Kc curves for two sugarbeet parcels are lower than standard FAO Kc and the authors conclude that use of standard FAO-56 Kc would result in over-irrigation, with supplied volumes following the satellite CWR trend; Section 5.3 Fig 16 - satellite citrus Kc consistent with FAO tables on average, and farm-scale satellite volumes close to measured applications (2.8 vs 3.1 Ml/ha citrus, 2.8 vs 2.7 vines); Section 5.1 - IRRISAT CWR (3500-4500 m3/ha maize) below applied volumes, with reduction of volumes reported. Q4: Figs 9, 12, 15 (LAI vs field LAI) and Fig 2 (ETcrop vs eddy covariance) measure the intermediate variables linking RS estimation to improved irrigation volumes. Q5: results reported separately for Campania, Marchfeld and Bookpurnong (Sections 5.1-5.3). Q6: Fig 11 district-level (1200 ha) comparison; Section 5.2 irrigation-scheme-level CWR vs distributed volumes in Marchfeld; Section 5.3 farm-scale cumulative volumes. Q7: Section 5.1 - adoption and efficiency gains linked by the authors to farm size above 10-12 ha, economic resources and metering-based water pricing; Section 6 - savings require convincing farmers to limit applications within ETcrop, and user feedback is essential. Q8: Section 5.1 scarce field data for comparison; Section 5.2 missing crop management/soil data, incomplete image coverage of the season; Section 5.3 comparison excludes above-average rainfall and further validation needed for tree crops; Section 5.1 LAI underestimation above 3.5 due to saturation.
rows.notes: The study estimates ETcrop under standard (well-watered) conditions and an analytical Kc, not actual Kc/Kcb or actual ET as named in the passage, and does not measure WPET; water saving is asserted from the comparison of satellite CWR with applied volumes rather than measured as a before/after reduction. Q3 no: single comparison method (advised vs metered volumes). Q9 no: Fig 16 reports <U+00B1>SD only for satellite citrus Kc, not for water saving; Fig 14 shading is a range between total- and effective-precipitation CWR, not a dispersion of the saving result; LAI RMSE is a validation error.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is largely a description of an operational service with case-study results; quantitative evidence on water saving is thin and partly based on water managers' estimates rather than the authors' own measurements.
